nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why is it important to have effective protected areas in Uganda?
nodes.answer: It is important to have effective protected areas to prevent serious biodiversity loss.
nodes.paragraph: 2016). Annual popula- tion growth of 3% (World Bank 2022) will likely increase pressures on land as demand for food and housing increases. Future socio-economic scenarios in Uganda therefore point towards fur - ther agricultural intensification and expansion, and the urgent need for effective protected areas to prevent serious biodiversity loss (Van Soes- bergen et al. 2016). To achieve this, protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures must be sufficiently representative of the national biodiversity, with a specific focus on biodiversity elements that are irreplaceable and/or critical for human well-being and global health. However, our understanding of useful plant species distributions and their representa- tion within the protected area network is limited due to the lack of a thorough assessment of plant species diversity and distribution in Uganda. It is, therefore, crucial to investigate plant species distribution patterns at finer resolutions to cre- ate an effective management strategy and inform policymakers and conservation practitioners. Addressing this gap, the current authors, together with a network of Ugandan biodiver - sity scientists and conservation practitioners, are actively undertaking identification of IPAs in Uganda, implementing all three IPA criteria 2025] O SULLIVAN ET AL.

nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What key management recommendation was made to prevent the extinction of the swift parrot?
nodes.answer: The management and protection of known swift parrot habitat at the landscape scale.
nodes.paragraph: By 2015, estimates of a severe population decline33 resulted in uplisting the swift parrot to Critically Endangered 34. A key management recommendation to avert extinction was the management and protection of known swift parrot habitat at the landscape scale with the goal of achieving a sustained population increase over 10 years. Nevertheless, the swift parrot population has continued to decline25, with fewer than 500 individuals remaining35. Recently, the Australian Government committed to averting extinction of swift parrots36,37, which calls into question whether forest policies currently in place across Tasmania support or exacerbate the swift parrot S negative population trajectory38. Moreover, Australia has signed global commitments to halt forest degradation and deforestation by 2030 (i.e. the Glasgow Leaders Declaration on Forests and Land Use) 39. To date, no quantitative range-wide assessment of habitat loss has been undertaken for the swift parrot, although it has been a listed action in recovery plans for more than a decade40,41. Quantifying forest degradation and stand-disturbance (e.g. partial canopy loss, height reduction, thinning) in landscapes that remain forested (by regenerating woody growth) presents challenges.
